lec05kp05-u01-p1-title.name: u01-p1-title
lec05kp05-u01-p1-title.text: In practice we only have labelled points: first split them into two groups with a master unit

lec05kp05-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp05-u01-p1-bridge.text: The three-layer construction of the previous KP knew the equations of the target regions, but in practice we only have labelled points. With the four XOR points, how can we start building a network from points?

lec05kp05-u01-p1-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp05-master
lec05kp05-u01-p1-fig1.text: The four XOR points with the master line z1=f(x1+x2-0.5): the 1 group above the line holds (0,1), (1,0) and (1,1), and only (0,0) in the lower left is in the 0 group.

image.alt: The four XOR points with the master line z1=f(x1+x2-0.5): the 1 group above the line holds (0,1), (1,0) and (1,1), and only (0,0) in the lower left is in the 0 group.

lec05kp05-u01-p1-c1.name: u01-p1-c1
lec05kp05-u01-p1-c1.text: **Situation**: only four points and their labels (circle is A, square is B), no equations of regions, so first try one line.

lec05kp05-u01-p1-term:主要節點.name: term:Master unit
lec05kp05-u01-p1-term:主要節點.text: **Master unit**: the first unit of a layer, in charge of classifying; it splits all points into a group with output 1 and a group with output 0. Here $z_1=f(x_1+x_2-0.5)$, where $f(t)=1$ if $t>0$ and 0 otherwise.

lec05kp05-u01-p1-q.name: u01-p1-q
lec05kp05-u01-p1-q.text: **To answer**: after the split, which group is still not clean?

lec05kp05-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp05-u01-p2-title.text: The master gets only 3 of 4 right: its 1 group holds two A and one B

lec05kp05-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp05-u01-p2-bridge.text: The master unit splits the four points into two groups. Which group has both classes, and how many points does the master get right on its own?

lec05kp05-u01-p2-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp05-mixed
lec05kp05-u01-p2-fig1.text: The same picture with red rings on the three points (0,1), (1,0), (1,1) of the 1 group, two A and one B, the mixed group; (0,0) is B and correct.

image.alt: The same picture with red rings on the three points (0,1), (1,0), (1,1) of the 1 group, two A and one B, the mixed group; (0,0) is B and correct.

lec05kp05-u01-p2-term:混雜群.name: term:Mixed group
lec05kp05-u01-p2-term:混雜群.text: **Mixed group**: an output group that contains points of both classes.

lec05kp05-u01-p2-c.name: u01-p2-c
lec05kp05-u01-p2-c.text: **Result**: $(0,0)$ alone is in the 0 group (B, correct). The 1 group is $(0,1)$, $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$, all called A: the two A are right and the B at $(1,1)$ is wrong. The master gets 3 points right.

lec05kp05-u01-p2-q.name: u01-p2-q
lec05kp05-u01-p2-q.text: **To answer**: can we deal with just these three points and split off the upper-right B?

lec05kp05-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp05-u01-p3-title.text: Add an ancillary unit trained on the three mixed points only, to split off the upper-right B

lec05kp05-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp05-u01-p3-bridge.text: To split off the upper-right B of the mixed group we only need to handle these three points. For a new unit, how should its formula be set?

lec05kp05-u01-p3-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp05-anc
lec05kp05-u01-p3-fig1.text: The solid line is the master unit and the violet dashed line is the ancillary unit z2=f(1.5-x1-x2): (0,1) and (1,0) score 0.5 and (1,1) scores -0.5.

image.alt: The solid line is the master unit and the violet dashed line is the ancillary unit z2=f(1.5-x1-x2): (0,1) and (1,0) score 0.5 and (1,1) scores -0.5.

lec05kp05-u01-p3-term:輔助節點.name: term:Ancillary unit
lec05kp05-u01-p3-term:輔助節點.text: **Ancillary unit**: a new unit trained only on the points of a mixed group; it gives every point one more bit that helps tell the classes apart inside that group.

lec05kp05-u01-p3-f.name: u01-p3-f
lec05kp05-u01-p3-f.text: **Here** $z_2=f(1.5-x_1-x_2)$: $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$ score $0.5$ and get bit 1; $(1,1)$ scores $-0.5$ and gets bit 0.

lec05kp05-u01-p3-n.name: u01-p3-n
lec05kp05-u01-p3-n.text: **Note**: $(0,0)$ is not in the mixed group and takes no part in training; its $z_2=f(1.5)=1$ is just a value computed along the way.

lec05kp05-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp05-u01-p4-title.text: With the extra bit the codes are 01, 11, 11, 10 and different classes no longer share a code

lec05kp05-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp05-u01-p4-bridge.text: The ancillary unit gives every point one more bit. Putting the bits of the master unit and the ancillary unit together, what are the codes of the four points?

lec05kp05-u01-p4-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp05-codes
lec05kp05-u01-p4-fig1.text: The two-bit codes z1z2 of the four points: (0,0) is 01, (0,1) and (1,0) are 11, and (1,1) is 10.

image.alt: The two-bit codes z1z2 of the four points: (0,0) is 01, (0,1) and (1,0) are 11, and (1,1) is 10.

lec05kp05-u01-p4-term:純化.name: term:Purification
lec05kp05-u01-p4-term:純化.text: **Purification**: adding bits so that points of different classes no longer share exactly the same code.

lec05kp05-u01-p4-n.name: u01-p4-n
lec05kp05-u01-p4-n.text: **One code per class is not required**: B occupies the two codes 01 and 10, which is fine; as long as different classes share no code it is purified.

lec05kp05-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp05-u01-p5-title.text: On the new codes, one new master unit classifies all four points

lec05kp05-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp05-u01-p5-bridge.text: After coding, different classes no longer share a code. In the new $(z_1,z_2)$ plane, is one line enough?

lec05kp05-u01-p5-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp05-code-plane
lec05kp05-u01-p5-fig1.text: The new (z1,z2) plane: the two A points merge at 11, B is at 01 and 10, 00 is hollow with no point; the line z1+z2=1.5 separates 11 from the other two codes.

image.alt: The new (z1,z2) plane: the two A points merge at 11, B is at 01 and 10, 00 is hollow with no point; the line z1+z2=1.5 separates 11 from the other two codes.

lec05kp05-u01-p5-a.name: u01-p5-a
lec05kp05-u01-p5-a.text: **New master unit**: replacing every point by its code $(z_1,z_2)$ moves it to this new plane (00 has no point). Take $z_1+z_2-1.5$: above 0 means A, otherwise B.

lec05kp05-u01-p5-b.name: u01-p5-b
lec05kp05-u01-p5-b.text: **Substitute code by code**: 11 gives $1+1-1.5=0.5$, A; 01 gives $0+1-1.5=-0.5$ and 10 gives $1+0-1.5=-0.5$, B.

lec05kp05-u01-p5-c.name: u01-p5-c
lec05kp05-u01-p5-c.text: **Result**: all four points are right. Merging the two A points at 11 is harmless because they are the same class.

lec05kp05-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp05-u01-p6-title.text: Why it stops: the mixed group shrinks, correct points increase, and the number of points is finite

lec05kp05-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp05-u01-p6-bridge.text: The new master unit got all four points right and the mixed group is gone. Why can we be sure such a process stops?

lec05kp05-u01-p6-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp05-progress
lec05kp05-u01-p6-fig1.text: Bar chart: with the master only, 3 points in the mixed group and 3 correct; after the ancillary and the new master, 0 mixed points and 4 correct; the dashed line marks N=4.

image.alt: Bar chart: with the master only, 3 points in the mixed group and 3 correct; after the ancillary and the new master, 0 mixed points and 4 correct; the dashed line marks N=4.

lec05kp05-u01-p6-a.name: u01-p6-a
lec05kp05-u01-p6-a.text: **Progress one**: within a layer, the mixed group that still needs refining strictly shrinks. Here it goes from 3 points to 0.

lec05kp05-u01-p6-b.name: u01-p6-b
lec05kp05-u01-p6-b.text: **Progress two**: let $C_k$ be the number of points the master of layer $k$ gets right. Under a suitable inter-layer construction the new master keeps the points the old one got right and gets at least one more: $C_{k+1}\ge C_k+1$. Here $C$ rises from 3 to 4.

lec05kp05-u01-p6-c.name: u01-p6-c
lec05kp05-u01-p6-c.text: **Because it is finite**: $C_k\le N$ is an integer and cannot increase forever, so it stops. Note that 3→0 counts points in the mixed group, not an error rate.

lec05kp05-u01-p7-title.name: u01-p7-title
lec05kp05-u01-p7-title.text: Stopping has conditions: labels must not contradict, and all correct only means these points

lec05kp05-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp05-u01-p7-bridge.text: Stopping relies on the mixed group shrinking and correct points increasing. When is this progress blocked, and what does all correct really mean?

lec05kp05-u01-p7-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp05-conflict
lec05kp05-u01-p7-fig1.text: One input labelled both A and B: a circle and a square on the same location with a red ring; the network has only one output for one input.

image.alt: One input labelled both A and B: a circle and a square on the same location with a red ring; the network has only one output for one input.

lec05kp05-u01-p7-a.name: u01-p7-a
lec05kp05-u01-p7-a.text: **Blocked case**: two identical inputs labelled with different classes. A deterministic network has one output for one input, so it cannot get both right.

lec05kp05-u01-p7-b.name: u01-p7-b
lec05kp05-u01-p7-b.text: **Not every addition works**: nodes must be added by rule to get strict progress; adding neurons arbitrarily does not guarantee termination.

lec05kp05-u01-p7-c.name: u01-p7-c
lec05kp05-u01-p7-c.text: **What all correct means**: it concerns only the points given, and guarantees neither correct answers at unseen locations nor a small network.

lec05kp05-u01-p7-q.name: u01-p7-q
lec05kp05-u01-p7-q.text: **Next**: can we fix the architecture first and then learn the weights with a cost function? (the next KP)

lec05kp05-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp05-u01-p8-title.text: Extension: another route (nearest neighbour): compare distances to two training points by their bisector, still one line

lec05kp05-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp05-u01-p8-bridge.text: All correct only means these points are all correct, and there is another route from points: compare distances to training points directly. For two points, how can the line of 'equally near' be written?

lec05kp05-u01-p8-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp05-nearest
lec05kp05-u01-p8-fig1.text: Two training points a=(0,0) (A) and b=(1,0) (B) with the perpendicular bisector x1=0.5 at equal distance from both.

image.alt: Two training points a=(0,0) (A) and b=(1,0) (B) with the perpendicular bisector x1=0.5 at equal distance from both.

lec05kp05-u01-p8-a.name: u01-p8-a
lec05kp05-u01-p8-a.text: **Equal distance**: expanding $\lVert\mathbf x-\mathbf a\rVert^2=\lVert\mathbf x-\mathbf b\rVert^2$ cancels the quadratic term and gives $2(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)^T\mathbf x=\lVert\mathbf b\rVert^2-\lVert\mathbf a\rVert^2$, a line.

lec05kp05-u01-p8-b.name: u01-p8-b
lec05kp05-u01-p8-b.text: **Example and cost**: $\mathbf a=(0,0)$ and $\mathbf b=(1,0)$ give $2x_1=1$, that is $x_1=0.5$. $N$ points have at most $N(N-1)/2$ pairs, so comparisons can grow quadratically; this is not a minimal network size.

lec05kp05-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp05-u01-p9-title.text: Extension: three layers suffice for purified codes, which is not a depth bound for the growth

lec05kp05-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp05-u01-p9-bridge.text: The nearest neighbour route must compare distances for many pairs of points, and the network is not minimal. How does the three-layer construction of KP04 relate to the layer-by-layer growth here?

lec05kp05-u01-p9-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp05-layers
lec05kp05-u01-p9-fig1.text: Schematic: inputs of later layers are binary codes, and detectors plus OR are enough (three layers); a layer-by-layer growth procedure has no stated bound on the number of layers.

image.alt: Schematic: inputs of later layers are binary codes, and detectors plus OR are enough (three layers); a layer-by-layer growth procedure has no stated bound on the number of layers.

lec05kp05-u01-p9-a.name: u01-p9-a
lec05kp05-u01-p9-a.text: **Why three layers suffice**: inputs after the first layer are binary codes, and KP04's detectors plus OR can classify the purified codes.

lec05kp05-u01-p9-b.name: u01-p9-b
lec05kp05-u01-p9-b.text: **But it does not mean**: this only shows that a suitable three-layer representation exists; a layer-by-layer growth procedure is not guaranteed to stop within three layers.

lec05kp05-u01-p9-c.name: u01-p9-c
lec05kp05-u01-p9-c.text: **Keep two things apart**: existence (which architecture is enough) and a depth guarantee for a procedure (how many layers this method grows) are not the same theorem.

lec05kp05-u01-p10-title.name: u01-p10-title
lec05kp05-u01-p10-title.text: Extension: practice, recount the mixed group and explain why 3 to 0 is not an error rate

lec05kp05-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec05kp05-u01-p10-bridge.text: Whether three layers suffice and how many layers the growth reaches are two things. Back to the four points of the example: is the mixed group going from 3 points to 0 really an error rate?

lec05kp05-u01-p10-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp05-master
lec05kp05-u01-p10-fig1.text: The four XOR points with the master line z1=f(x1+x2-0.5): the 1 group above the line holds (0,1), (1,0) and (1,1), and only (0,0) in the lower left is in the 0 group.

image.alt: The four XOR points with the master line z1=f(x1+x2-0.5): the 1 group above the line holds (0,1), (1,0) and (1,1), and only (0,0) in the lower left is in the 0 group.

lec05kp05-u01-p10-q1.name: u01-p10-q1
lec05kp05-u01-p10-q1.text: **Question 1**: group the four points by their full code, list the labels of each group and count the points in mixed groups.

lec05kp05-u01-p10-h1.name: u01-p10-h1
lec05kp05-u01-p10-h1.text: **Hint**: first write down which points have each of the codes 01, 11 and 10.

lec05kp05-u01-p10-q2.name: u01-p10-q2
lec05kp05-u01-p10-q2.text: **Question 2**: if one input appears with contradictory labels, can adding more nodes classify both correctly? Explain with deterministic outputs.

lec05kp05-u01-p11-title.name: u01-p11-title
lec05kp05-u01-p11-title.text: Extension: worked solution of questions 1 and 2

lec05kp05-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp05-u01-p11-bridge.text: The practice recounts the mixed group and asks about contradictory labels. What are the answers?

lec05kp05-u01-p11-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp05-groups
lec05kp05-u01-p11-fig1.text: Left: grouped by the master bit only, the 0 group is one B and the 1 group is two A and one B (mixed, 3 points); right: grouped by the full code, 01 is B, 11 is two A and 10 is B, all pure, 0 mixed points.

image.alt: Left: grouped by the master bit only, the 0 group is one B and the 1 group is two A and one B (mixed, 3 points); right: grouped by the full code, 01 is B, 11 is two A and 10 is B, all pure, 0 mixed points.

lec05kp05-u01-p11-a1.name: u01-p11-a1
lec05kp05-u01-p11-a1.text: **Question 1 (grouping)**: by master bit: $\{(0,0)\}$ is B, pure; $\{(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)\}$ is A, A, B, mixed, 3 points. By full code: 01: B; 11: A, A; 10: B, all pure, 0 mixed.

lec05kp05-u01-p11-a3.name: u01-p11-a3
lec05kp05-u01-p11-a3.text: **Question 1 (not an error rate)**: 3→0 counts points still mixed, not wrong answers. The master alone is wrong on 1 point (the B at $(1,1)$).

lec05kp05-u01-p11-a4.name: u01-p11-a4
lec05kp05-u01-p11-a4.text: **Question 2**: the same input gives the same output, so a deterministic network gives one answer and cannot be right for both A and B.

steps.label: Grow from points
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Main line 7 pages plus 4 extension pages (not timed). Self-study deck, English version. Rewritten under CLARITY.md C12 to C18: plain words before terms, titles that state the point, pages linked by questions, a figure on every spatial page. These notes are public with the file and contain no student IDs, grades or exam questions.

steps.label: Split once first
steps.speakerNotes: The three-layer construction of the previous KP assumed we know the equations of the target regions, while in practice we usually have only labelled points. This page takes the four XOR points and starts building from points: first one master unit, the first unit of a layer in charge of classification, splits the four points into a group with output 1 and a group with output 0. The orange line in the figure is z1 = f(x1+x2-0.5): above it is the 1 group, and only (0,0) in the lower left is in the 0 group. After the split we ask which group is still not clean. The next page looks at that.

steps.label: Find the mixed group
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page split the four points into two groups with the master unit. This page checks them: the 0 group holds only (0,0), a B, and is fine; the 1 group holds (0,1), (1,0) and (1,1), all called A by the master, so the two A are right and the B at the upper right (1,1) is wrong; the master alone gets 3 points right. An output group that contains both classes is a mixed group, and the red rings mark its three points. Next we ask whether we can deal with just these three points and split off the upper-right B.

steps.label: Add an ancillary
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page found the mixed group, with three points in the 1 group. This page adds a new unit called an ancillary unit: it is trained only on the points of the mixed group and gives every point one more bit. The formula here is z2 = f(1.5 - x1 - x2), with the violet dashed line as its boundary: (0,1) and (1,0) score 0.5 and get bit 1; the upper-right (1,1) scores minus 0.5 and gets bit 0, so the B is split off. (0,0) is not in the mixed group and took no part in training; its z2 of 1 is just a value computed along the way. This is a mechanism demonstration, not a recorded run of some training algorithm. Next we put the two bits together.

steps.label: Two-bit codes
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page's ancillary unit gave every point one more bit. This page puts the master bit z1 and the ancillary bit z2 together: (0,0) gets 01, (0,1) and (1,0) both get 11, and (1,1) gets 10. The figure labels each point with its code. Adding a bit so that points of different classes no longer share exactly the same code is called purification. Purification does not require one code per class: B occupying the two codes 01 and 10 is fine. Next we ask whether one line is enough on the new codes.

steps.label: New master correct
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page replaced the four points by two-bit codes, and different classes no longer share a code. This page uses a new master unit on the new z1-z2 plane: z1 plus z2 minus 1.5, above 0 means A. In the figure there are three locations: 11 scores 0.5, A; 01 and 10 both score minus 0.5, B; the code 00 has no point. So all four points are right. This is the same trick as the two-layer XOR of KP02, except that the extra bit now grew out of the mixed group. Next we ask why this kind of procedure stops.

steps.label: Why it stops
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page's new master got all four points right and the mixed group disappeared. This page asks why such a process stops. There are two kinds of progress: first, within a layer the mixed group that still needs refining strictly shrinks, here from 3 points to 0; second, let $C_k$ be the number of points the master of layer $k$ gets right. Under a suitable inter-layer construction the new master keeps the points the old one got right and gets at least one more, so with C the number of correct points, C of the next layer is at least C of this layer plus 1, here from 3 to 4. Because C is an integer not above the number of points N it cannot increase forever, so the process stops. Note that the red bar in the figure is the number of points in the mixed group, not an error rate. This is the stopping reason when the conditions hold, not a claim that it always stops. The next page says what the conditions are.

steps.label: Conditions apply
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said stopping relies on the mixed group shrinking and correct points increasing. This page asks when the progress is blocked: two identical inputs labelled with different classes, shown in the figure as a square and a circle on top of each other; a deterministic network has one output for one input and cannot get both right, so such label conflicts must be excluded. Also, nodes must be added by rule; adding neurons arbitrarily does not guarantee termination. Finally a reminder: all correct concerns only the points given, and guarantees neither correct answers at unseen locations nor a small network. The main line ends here. The next KP asks whether we can fix the architecture first and learn the weights with a cost function. The extension that follows first looks at another route starting from the training points.

steps.label: Extension: nearest
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page reminded us that all correct only means these points are all correct. This page looks at another route that starts from the training points: compare distances with the perpendicular bisector of two training points. Expanding the squared distances to a and to b cancels the common quadratic term and leaves 2 times (b minus a) transposed times x equal to the squared length of b minus the squared length of a, a line. With a equal to (0,0) and b equal to (1,0) we get 2 x1 equal to 1, that is x1 equal to 0.5, exactly between the two points, the orange line in the figure. Later AND forms local regions and OR merges same-class regions. N points have at most N(N-1)/2 pairs, so comparisons can grow quadratically, but this is not a minimal network size. This is only one pairwise comparison, not a full nearest-neighbour network experiment. A last question: can we fix the architecture first and learn the weights with a cost function? That is the next KP.

steps.label: Extension: 3 layers
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page's nearest-neighbour route may need many comparisons and the network is not minimal. This extension explains how the three-layer construction of KP04 relates to layer-by-layer growth: inputs after the first layer are binary codes, so KP04's detectors plus OR can classify the purified codes, which shows that a suitable three-layer representation is enough. But it does not mean that any layer-by-layer growth procedure stops within three layers. Existence and a depth guarantee for a procedure are two things, not the same theorem. This page is an extension and is not timed. The next page is a practice.

steps.label: Extension: practice
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said that three layers sufficing and how many layers the growth reaches are two things. This page asks the students to practise on the four points of the example. Question 1: group the four points by their full code, list the labels of each group, count the points in mixed groups and explain why 3 dropping to 0 is not an error rate; question 2: if one input appears with contradictory labels, can adding more nodes get both right. The figure shows the split by the master unit. Hint: first write down which points have each of the codes 01, 11 and 10. The next page gives the complete worked solution.

steps.label: Extension: solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page posed questions 1 and 2 and this page is the complete worked solution. Grouping: looking only at the master bit, the 0 group holds just (0,0), label B, pure; the 1 group is (0,1), (1,0) and (1,1) with labels A, A, B, mixed, 3 points in all. Grouping by full code: 01 is B, 11 is A and A, 10 is B, every group is pure and the mixed group has 0 points. The drop from 3 to 0 counts points still mixed, while an error rate counts wrong answers; here the master alone is wrong on just 1 point, so they are different things. Question 2: the same input always gets the same output, so a deterministic network gives one answer and cannot be right for both A and B; with contradictory labels it cannot be all correct. KP05 ends here and the next KP fixes the architecture and learns the weights.

metadata.title: Pattern Recognition, Chapter 4, KP05: growing a network from training points (undergraduate, self-study)
